answer.sourceLine: Confirmed word for word. It is Ruskin’s declared summation of the whole series — section 77 of Essay IV, “Ad Valorem,” the last of the four essays he published in the Cornhill Magazine in 1860 and reissued as the book Unto This Last in 1862 — and it is there in the full text, introduced by the sentence Ruskin wrote to frame it: “I desire, in closing the series of introductory papers, to leave this one great fact clearly stated.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Unto This Last”: Four Essays on the First Principles of Political Economy
Essay IV, “Ad Valorem,” section 77 — Ruskin’s declared summation of the series
Cornhill Magazine, 1860; in book form London: Smith, Elder & Co., 1862
Written in English — no translation involved

source.excerpt: I left this question to the reader’s thought two months ago, choosing rather that he should work it out for himself than have it sharply stated to him. But now, the ground being sufficiently broken … I desire, in closing the series of introductory papers, to leave this one great fact clearly stated. THERE IS NO WEALTH BUT LIFE. Life, including all its powers of love, of joy, and of admiration. That country is the richest which nourishes the greatest number of noble and happy human beings; that man is richest who, having perfected the functions of his own life to the utmost, has also the widest helpful influence, both personal and by means of his possessions, over the lives of others.
trail: Searched the complete text of Unto This Last, and Other Essays on Political Economy at Project Gutenberg ↗ and found the sentence verbatim in Essay IV, “Ad Valorem” — introduced by Ruskin’s own framing, “I desire, in closing the series of introductory papers, to leave this one great fact clearly stated.”
Cross-checked against an independently scanned printing: the 1901 T. Y. Crowell edition ↗, introduced by Richard T. Ely, carries the same passage as “There is no Wealth but Life.”
Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ lists the quotation under Unto This Last (1860) and gives the same placement: Essay IV, “Ad Valorem,” section 77.

Publication history taken from Ruskin’s own preface, which states that the four essays “were published eighteen months ago in the Cornhill Magazine”, and from the Internet Archive record for the first book edition ↗ — London: Smith, Elder and Co., 65 Cornhill, 1862.
source.excerptNote: Editions typeset the emphasis differently: the Project Gutenberg transcription of the 1912 Ward, Lock text renders the sentence in full capitals, while the 1901 T. Y. Crowell edition prints “There is no Wealth but Life.” The emphasis is Ruskin’s; the words are identical.

author.name: John Ruskin
author.heading: Who was John Ruskin?
author.metaLine: 1819–1900 · English art critic, draughtsman and social reformer
author.bio: Ruskin was the most influential art critic of Victorian Britain — the champion of Turner and the Pre-Raphaelites, author of Modern Painters and The Stones of Venice — who then turned the same moral scrutiny on the economy. He argued that the discipline of political economy had never properly defined its central word, wealth, and that any definition worth having would have to be measured in human lives rather than in stock. The four essays he wrote to make that case were furiously unpopular at the time and became, within a generation, some of the most quoted social criticism in English.

misattribution.heading: Ruskin gets blamed for a lot he never wrote
misattribution.intro: This one is real — which makes it the exception. John Ruskin is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for invented business-wisdom quotes, and the lines pinned to him are usually the ones nobody can find anywhere in the thirty-nine volumes of his collected works. Three of the best-known examples:

items.who: Not Ruskin — earliest in print is J. A. Richards, 1901
items.why: “There is hardly anything in the world that some man cannot make a little worse and sell a little cheaper…” Quote Investigator ↗ finds it first in print in February 1901, in a letter from a correspondent named J. A. Richards to the trade journal Profitable Advertising — with no attribution to Ruskin, who had died in January 1900. The Ruskin credit only appears in October 1926. QI calls Richards the “top candidate” rather than the certain author, allowing that he may have been repeating a formulation already in circulation. Ruskin scholar George P. Landow went looking for this line in the works where Ruskin discusses value and could not find it, reporting ↗ that the Ruskin Centre at Lancaster has “never been able to identify it as being by Ruskin.”
“When love and skill work together, expect a masterpiece.” Wikiquote ↗ lists this under Misattributed and identifies the real source as Charles Reade’s novel Put Yourself in His Place.

The “common law of business balance” passage — “It’s unwise to pay too much, but it’s worse to pay too little…” — is, per Wikiquote ↗ citing the Yale Book of Quotations, widely attributed to Ruskin but never sourced to any of his works.

misattribution.truthLine: “There is no wealth but life” is the rare Ruskin line online that survives checking: the words, the emphasis and the paragraph around them are all his, and you can read them in the full text of Unto This Last ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Ruskin wrote the four essays that became Unto This Last for the Cornhill Magazine in 1860, and the readership loathed them. His own preface to the 1862 book is blunt about it: the essays “were reprobated in a violent manner, as far as I could hear, by most of the readers they met with.” The series stopped at four. So the fourth essay was written knowing it was the last, and part-way through it Ruskin broke off to state the one thing he most wanted on the record — not a slogan about money, but a definition. Wealth, he insisted, is not the stuff in the warehouse; it is the life that stuff sustains.

In the same preface Ruskin called these essays “the truest, rightest-worded, and most serviceable things I have ever written,” and said of the last of them that it “is probably the best I shall ever write.” That judgement has largely held up. The six words have since been carved, printed and hashtagged more or less continuously — usually without the two sentences that follow, which are the ones doing the actual definitional work.
context.detailsSummary: The long afterlife of one paragraph
detailsBody: The book found its most consequential reader in South Africa. According to Wikipedia’s account of the work ↗, Gandhi encountered Unto This Last in March 1904 through Henry Polak, and in 1908 rendered it into Gujarati under the title Sarvodaya (“Well Being of All”); Valji Govindji Desai translated that paraphrase back into English in 1951 as Unto This Last: A Paraphrase.

The clipped six-word version is not a misquotation — it is Ruskin’s own emphasised sentence, and he set it off deliberately. But the sentences immediately after it are the definition: the richest country is the one “which nourishes the greatest number of noble and happy human beings,” and the richest man the one whose perfected life has “the widest helpful influence” over the lives of others. Quoted alone, the line reads as sentiment; quoted whole, it reads as an argument about how to keep national accounts.

sourcesVerified.claim: The full text of Unto This Last contains "THERE IS NO WEALTH BUT LIFE. Life, including all its powers of love, of joy, and of admiration..." in Essay IV, "Ad Valorem" — about three-quarters of the way through the essay, not at its close, with several further sections following; the preface states the four essays were published in the Cornhill Magazine and that the last of them is "probably the best I shall ever write."
Project Gutenberg ebook #36541 is Unto This Last, and Other Essays on Political Economy by John Ruskin, distributed as public domain in the USA.

Internet Archive item untothislastfour01rusk is the 1901 New York, T. Y. Crowell edition of Unto This Last with an introduction by Richard T. Ely; its scanned text reads "There is no Wealth but Life. Life, including all its powers of love, of joy, and of admiration."
Internet Archive item ruskinuntothislast is "Unto this last": four essays on the first principles of political economy, published London: Smith, Elder and Co., 65, Cornhill, 1862.

Wikiquote lists the quotation under Unto This Last (1860) with the citation Essay IV: "Ad Valorem," section 77; its Disputed section covers "a little worse and sell a little cheaper" and the "common law of business balance" (citing the Yale Book of Quotations), and its Misattributed section attributes "When love and skill work together, expect a masterpiece" to Charles Reade's Put Yourself in His Place.

Quote Investigator finds the earliest print appearance of "There is hardly anything in the world that some man cannot make a little worse and sell a little cheaper" in February 1901 in Profitable Advertising, in a letter from J. A. Richards, with no Ruskin attribution until October 1926; Ruskin died in January 1900.

George P. Landow's Victorian Web page is about "There is hardly anything in the world that someone cannot make a little worse and sell a little cheaper" — and only that line — reporting that he could not find it in the works where Ruskin discusses value, and quoting the Ruskin Centre at Lancaster: "we have been asked many times about this quote, or similar versions of it, and have never been able to identify it as being by Ruskin."

Gandhi discovered Unto This Last in March 1904 through Henry Polak, translated it into Gujarati in 1908 as Sarvodaya, and Valji Govindji Desai translated it back into English in 1951 as Unto This Last: A Paraphrase; the book edition appeared in 1862 after magazine publication in 1860.

John Ruskin lived 8 February 1819 – 20 January 1900, was an English writer, art historian, art critic, draughtsman, philanthropist and social reformer, and the article quotes "There is no wealth but life. Life, including all its powers of love, of joy, and of admiration."
